subject: astronomy
title: Neutron Stars and Pulsars
welcome_lead: When even electrons cannot hold gravity back.
meta_desc: A-Level Astronomy: neutron stars, pulsars, TOV limit.
final_note: A neutron star is the universe's smallest visible object.

concepts.def: Remnant supported by neutron degeneracy pressure.
Rapidly rotating, magnetised neutron star with beamed emission.
Neutron star with extreme magnetic field.
Protons and electrons combining to form neutrons under extreme pressure.

walkthroughs.body_html: When a massive core exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit, electrons are forced into protons (neutronisation), forming a city-sized ball of neutrons just 10-20 km across but with mass between 1.4 and the TOV limit.

Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsar in 1967. A pulsar's strong magnetic field channels beams from its poles; spinning, it acts like a lighthouse with periods from milliseconds to seconds.
The Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit sets the maximum neutron-star mass at about 2-3 solar masses. Heavier remnants collapse into black holes.

mcqs.q: What defines a star as being on the 'main sequence'?
options: It is the hottest stage.
It fuses hydrogen into helium in its core.
It is the largest stage of a star's life.
Because they are the brightest objects in the universe.

mcqs.q: What determines whether a star becomes a white dwarf or a neutron star?
options: Its colour during its main sequence phase.
It is the hottest stage.
Whether it has planets.
Its mass - low/medium mass becomes a white dwarf; massive stars produce neutron stars or black holes.

mcqs.q: Why are Type Ia supernovae used as 'standard candles'?
options: It is the hottest stage.
Because they happen at regular time intervals.
They have nearly uniform peak brightness, so their apparent brightness reveals distance.
Because they are the brightest objects in the universe.
